claims.text: The identity of X (Si, Mn, or Al) controls the stability of the high-temperature oxide scale on CrFeCoNiX.
X controls scale stability by changing diffusion kinetics and defect formation within the oxide.
A lower diffusivity mismatch and a stronger, more slowly growing oxide promote a coherent and persistent protective scale.
Al in CrFeCoNiAl is expected to form Al2O3.
Al addition will produce a coherent protective scale that persists above 900 °C.
Mn or Si additions cause faster cation or oxygen diffusion and higher oxide defect concentrations than Al.
The faster diffusion and higher defect concentrations attributed to Mn or Si cause stress buildup, cracking, and spallation.
The proposed comparison systematically replaces X with Si, Mn, or Al while holding the CrFeCoNi portion and processing conditions otherwise constant.
The comparison is conducted above 900 °C for approximately 12–24 hours in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
Oxide phase composition and structure evolve according to the constituent elements' environmental interactions and thermodynamic tendencies.
Diffusion mismatch produces internal stress distributions within the evolving oxide scale.
X alters the balance between outward metal-cation diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion at the alloy/oxide interface.
Atomic size and redox potential influence oxidation, with redox potential becoming dominant over time.
Al has a favorable redox potential and smaller atomic size that favor slow and uniform oxide growth.
An Al2O3 scale on CrFeCoNiAl will have low defect density and reduced internal stress.
Mn or Si promote rapid, heterogeneous oxide growth that increases defects and stress.
Under identical exposure conditions, CrFeCoNiAl will show slower oxide growth, lower defect density, lower stress, and less cracking or spallation than the Si- and Mn-containing alloys.
A neutral or less effective control composition will show faster oxide growth, higher internal stress, and greater spallation.
The hypothesis is scoped to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C for about 12–24 hours.
Minor composition changes and processing history may alter the quantitative oxide growth, defect, and stress differences.
